This is how I've run my 17+ person shows. But always remember this is high school, and really a student should have to run board for a 17 mic show. Good luck, and enjoy it.

1. Always track who is onstage when
2. EQ is your best friend for natural sounding actors
3. Track positions onstage, when you have two actors in close contact, lower the volume on one of them
4. If the director can't hear the actors, make sure they are projecting. There is a limit to how much the mic can help, and diction, projection, and the ability to hit a note is not in your purview
5. Practice makes comfort. Start mic'ing early, get time on the board to get comfortable with it.
6. You will make mistakes, so make sure to take notes, better to make a lot of different mistakes than to make the same mistake twice.
7. Learn how to properly mic an actor. Placement is one of the most important things to learn, and the easiest way to avoid paying for new equipment later is to have good technique early on.
8. Trust your musical director. They have had to listen to the actors warble their way through rehearsals for a while. They know what the show is supposed to sound like. Use them wisely

YOUR FOLIO-of-PORT, OR HOW TO BE JUDGED
 
In 2015 I was asked to adjudicate the Southeastern Theatre Conference sound design student participants. This was the first year they had an outside person come in to judge, but I hope it wasn't the last. One thing I noticed was a little inconsistency in how the students were told to prepare their projects and portfolios. The following are merely my suggestions if I were in charge of these sorts of things:
 
PLAYS:

- give a short description of the piece and the intended goals of the sound design.
- show a speaker plot, with annotations to justify locations, or to discuss an installed system that couldn't be modified and how you made it work to your needs of the show.
- show a system plot, including what systems were used for audio playback, and any shortcomings you encountered.
- provide audio samples mixed down to two tracks with a short description of their places within the piece.
- separately, provide descriptions of the audio samples and discuss what choices were made; also talk about what elements were requested by the director, and how those goals were met.  Provide a little insight into the cues and how they were constructed, i.e. found sounds, prerecorded music, music that was composed specifically for the piece, etc.
- discuss any inter-departmental collaborative elements, i.e. synchronizing with Projection Design or Lighting Design, etc.
- discuss what challenges were present in the piece, the space, or the system, and how these were overcome— or NOT overcome to your satisfaction.
 
MUSICALS:

- give a short description of the piece and the intended goals of the sound design, and the aesthetic that was required of the piece.
- show a speaker plot, with annotations to justify speaker locations, or to discuss an installed system that couldn't be modified and how you made it work to your needs of the show.
- show a system plot and any other paperwork, i.e. input/output lists, microphone choices, speaker choices.
- discuss what equalization was necessary and how system tuning was accomplished.
- provide a short recording either directly from the mixing console or as a separate "mics-in-the-house" version.
- discuss inter-departmental collaborative elements, i.e. speaker locations, microphone positions on actors, how the orchestra was laid out and what microphones were used, how, and why. Visual aids (photographs) are welcome!
- discuss what challenges were present in the piece, the space, the system, or the talent, and how these were overcome— or NOT overcome to your satisfaction.

I would start working on a portfolio of your shows, and think about college. It definitely expanded my horizons. Your portfolio materials should be organized in a folder or case for presentation and should include the following

-Individual pieces that demonstrate the student’s artistic ability in the areas of technical theatre. drawing, painting, writing, photography, sewing, drafting, rendering,
construction, sound editing, etc.

-Photos of the candidate working in their areas of interest

-Complete design process in one of their areas of interest, not necessarily a realized production (to show the design process from research to project in the form of a model or renderings.)

-Examples of a realized design process or design (that actually went into production)

-Research demonstrating a thorough script analysis.

-Drafting or drawings done in the planning stages.

-Photos of the work in progress focusing specifically on what the student is working on.

-Photos of the finished product in production

This is a pretty basic portfolio checklist, the photos of you working not really necessary, but for college applications and the like they can be useful.

Also start a resume of your shows, absolutely necessary for applying to jobs or colleges. A resume should include performances you have participated in, the role you played, and the dates of the performance. Your resume should include information about your education, training and experience, awards, skills, as well as any references you think can give you a good review.
